## The Letter from Tomorrow

Every night at 12:17 a.m., the mailman named Elias found a letter waiting in his bag.

Not from the local post office, and not from any of the townspeople. The envelopes were cream-colored, unstamped, and addressed in handwriting so neat it looked as though it had been copied from a dictionary. The postmark bore tomorrow’s date.

The first time it happened, Elias assumed he had made a mistake. The letter was addressed to a woman named Mara Venn, who lived in the yellow house at the end of Wren Street. He delivered it the next morning. At noon, he saw her standing in her garden, staring at the envelope as if it had bitten her.

“You shouldn’t have brought this,” she said.

“It came to me.”

“That isn’t what I meant.”

Elias had never been especially good at understanding what people meant. It was one of the qualities that had kept him in the postal service for twenty-three years. Letters were simpler. A letter said what it said, waited to be carried, and eventually arrived.

Mara opened hers with a knife. Inside was a single line:

**You will be offered the job on Thursday. Do not accept.**

Elias waited.

“What does that mean?” he asked.

“It means I won’t take it.”

“Then why would it warn you not to?”

Mara looked toward the hill where the town hall stood. “Because something will happen if I do.”

The next night, another letter arrived.

This one was addressed to the baker, Mr. Oren, and it said:

**Your daughter will come home on Friday. Let her.**

Mr. Oren read it twice, folded it carefully, and placed it beneath his flour tin. On Friday, his daughter returned after eleven years away. He wept, but did not let her go, though Elias never learned what that instruction had meant.

Letters continued arriving for the schoolteacher, the ferryman, the woman who ran the bookshop, the boy who repaired clocks. They were always brief. Sometimes warnings. Sometimes requests. Once, the letter delivered to the veterinarian said:

**Tell the brown dog you forgive him.**

No one in town owned a brown dog except the veterinarian.

Elias began to wonder who wrote them. The handwriting was identical, but the paper varied—some sheets were thick and rough, others thin as onion skin. One letter smelled faintly of woodsmoke. Another had a flower pressed into the fold.

Then, on the fourteenth night, he found an envelope with his own name.

His hands trembled as he opened it.

**You will find the letter in the church basement. Burn it.**

Elias did not go to the church.

He was not a brave man, exactly. He was a patient man, which in his experience amounted to much the same thing. Patient people could endure almost anything except being asked to make a decision.

For three days, he carried the letter in his coat pocket. It softened with his body heat. The ink faded. By the third evening, he could barely read it.

On the fourth, he went to the church.

The basement was cold and cluttered with old hymnbooks, broken furniture, and crates of Christmas decorations. Elias held the letter beneath a bulb and searched the walls. Behind a stack of folding chairs, he found a small door painted the same green as the basement walls.

The door was locked.

He considered forcing it, but instead he sat on the bottom step and waited.

Around midnight, someone came down the stairs.

It was Mara.

“Of course it’s you,” she said. “I wondered how long you would take.”

She took the letter from him, though her hands were steady and his were not.

“You burned yours,” she said.

“I didn’t.”

“I know. That’s why I came.”

She sat beside him on the step. For a while, neither spoke.

“I was offered the job,” Mara said. “The director’s job. I said no.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to know whether I could.”

Elias stared at the green door. “Did you?”

“No. But I liked finding out that I wanted to.”

At last, Mara opened the door.

The room beyond was small and entirely empty except for a wooden desk. On the desk lay a stack of letters, cream-colored and unmarked. The handwriting on all of them was the same.

“Is that where they come from?” Elias asked.

“No,” she said. “That’s where they go after they’re read.”

“And who writes them?”

Mara looked at him. “You do.”

The basement clock began to chime.

Elias felt the floor tilt beneath him. “I don’t write letters.”

“Not yet.”

The clock struck twelve. Mara picked up the stack, and suddenly the room filled with the scent of woodsmoke, wet earth, perfume, flour, and rain. Elias heard a hundred small sounds: a dog barking, a baby crying, an argument behind a closed door, a ship’s horn far out to sea.

“Do you want to see tomorrow?” Mara asked.

He thought of all the letters he had carried. All the small, impossible instructions. He thought of the woman who had returned home, the brown dog who had been forgiven, the questions people had carried like stones in their pockets.

“Yes,” he said.

Mara handed him the top envelope.

His name was on it, but beneath his name, instead of an address, was a single sentence:

**Whatever you do next will matter less than you fear and more than you hope.**

Elias opened the letter.

Outside, dawn began to gather over the rooftops of the town. Somewhere a kettle whistled. Somewhere a cart rattled over cobblestones. The mailman sat in a green room with a woman he had not yet met, holding the first letter he would ever deliver.

It was addressed to someone he loved.

He did not know their name, but he knew their street, their house, and the exact hour when they would open their door.

Elias smiled.

He had always been good at carrying things to where they belonged.
